title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction CostsLong-Horizon Coding Agents

paper.title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Context compaction lets long-horizon coding agents continue beyond their context windows, but can erase the state needed to finish a task. Prior evaluations measure efficiency, retained information, or end-to-end success, leaving the effect of a specific history replacement difficult to isolate. Compact-Bench pairs full-history and summary-only continuations from a shared repository state, and evaluates recurring details and successive production compactions. It covers 35 35 SWE-bench repairs, 146 146 agentic sessions, and 106 106 production chains. Across 14 14 summarizer backbones, stable damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% of 22 22 full-history successes: Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserves the most repairs, while DeepSeek-Flash damages the most. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, the Kimi Code prompt preserves the most task continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). LLM summaries retain at most 16.0 % 16.0\% of recurring details, compared with 79.1 % 79.1\% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7 % 15.7\% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13 / 14 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation. Code and data are available online.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Long-horizon coding agents accumulate instructions, tool observations, test results, and partial decisions. Compaction allows them to work beyond the context window, but the resulting summary must carry enough state to resume unfinished work. Long-context benchmarks test retrieval, reasoning, and generation from extended inputs ( Bai et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Hsieh et al., 2024 ; Shaham et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Kuratov et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ) , and information access can depend on input position ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . Agent histories add a further requirement: preserving which actions have been taken, which hypotheses have been rejected, and what remains to be done. End-to-end benchmarks evaluate repository repair, code generation, and interactive tool use ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024c ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . A final score, however, does not isolate the effect of replacing a history midway through a task. Recent compaction evaluations examine constraint loss, archived-fact retrieval, future-trajectory support, and execution instability; methods also learn or schedule summarization and remove observations ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Subramani, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Cim et al., 2026 ; Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . Compact-Bench targets the history replacement itself: it compares full-history and summary-only continuation at a shared boundary, then examines detail retention in real agent sessions. The benchmark asks: For the same task and pre-compaction state, how does continuation change when an agent receives only a summary instead of its full history? Task Preservation compares full-history and summary-only continuations from the same repository snapshot, using the same agent, step budget, and executable tests. Recurring-Detail Retention measures preservation of structured details that recur in later requests across 146 146 sessions ( 143 143 real and 3 3 simulator-synthesized). Production-Chain Retention follows these details across successive compactions in 106 106 real sessions. Together, the three evaluations connect controlled task outcomes with information retention in deployed workflows. Across 14 14 summarizer backbones, stable Task Preservation damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% of the 22 22 validated full-history successes, with Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserving the most repairs. Of 126 126 instance-backbone pairs damaged in the first round, 120 120 meet the three-run confirmation criterion. Task preservation and detail retention also distinguish different configurations: Kimi Code gives the most passing continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). Paired traces reveal a shared failure pattern: summaries can retain the target file and relevant strings while losing the progress needed to finish a repair. Overall, our contributions are: • We introduce Compact-Bench , a benchmark for evaluating whether context compaction preserves a coding agent’s ability to resume work. It combines controlled task continuations with recurring-detail and production-chain measurements. • We compare 14 14 summarizer backbones and 5 5 production prompts. Stable task damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% among 22 22 full-history successes, with Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserving the most repairs. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, Kimi Code preserves the most task continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), while Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). • We show that retained repair evidence does not guarantee successful continuation. Paired traces reveal failures even when summaries preserve target files and relevant code strings. Together with the different task-preservation and detail-retention leaders, this finding motivates evaluating compaction through both retained information and agent behavior. sections.heading: Direct evaluations of compaction.
sections.text: COMPINT evaluates side-constraint retention, LANTERN tests archived-conversation retrieval, and Slipstream checks summary support for subsequent trajectory steps ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Subramani, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . TRACE compares execution after restoring a shared environment, while Complexity Trap evaluates observation masking ( Min et al., 2026 ; Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . Compact-Bench combines fixed-boundary replay with a fourteen-backbone and five-prompt comparison, recurring-detail measurements, and repeated production boundaries. The replay links a specific history replacement to a change in task outcome.

sections.heading: Methods for agent histories and persistent memory.
sections.text: ReSum summarizes search trajectories; Context-Folding condenses completed subtasks; CompactionRL trains execution and summarization jointly; SelfCompact lets the agent choose when to compact; and parallel compaction summarizes separate blocks ( Wu et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026a ; Cim et al., 2026 ) . Persistent-memory methods maintain or retrieve information outside the active history, including MemoryBank, A-Mem, MemGPT, and retrieval-augmented generation ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Packer et al., 2023 ; Lewis et al., 2020 ) . LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and Beyond Prompts evaluate memory over extended or interleaved dialogue ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Maharana et al., 2024 ; Castillo-Bolado et al., 2024 ) . Our recurring-detail and production-chain tracks assess structured information that reappears after compaction in coding-agent workflows.

sections.heading: Prompt compression and summary evaluation.
sections.text: Prompt compression reduces input length through token selection (Selective Context, LLMLingua), question-aware selection (LongLLMLingua), distilled selection (LLMLingua-2), soft representations (Gist tokens, ICAE), and offline compression with adaptation (LLoCO) ( Li et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Mu et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2024 ) . RECOMP compresses retrieved passages; a survey organizes the broader method families ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Summary evaluation measures factual consistency and answerability, including Kryscinski et al., FEQA, and QuestEval; G-Eval uses LLM judgments for broader generation quality ( Kryscinski et al., 2020 ; Durmus et al., 2020 ; Scialom et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Compact-Bench extends the evaluation target to resuming agent work, combining executable outcomes with deterministic matching of recurring details.

sections.heading: 3.1 Evaluation Dimensions
sections.text: Let H H denote the serialized agent history immediately before a compaction boundary. The compaction method under test, denoted by C C , includes the summarizer and prompt together with the fixed serialization and truncation procedure described in Appendix G ; applying it to H H produces summary S = C ⁡ ( H ) S=C(H) . A compaction boundary is the point at which this replacement occurs. In Task Preservation, PRE continues with the full history H H , whereas POST continues with only S S . Both conditions start from the same repository working-tree snapshot, denoted by D D in Figure 1 . Task Preservation tests whether continuation from S S completes repairs that also succeed from H H . For each repair, Phase A caches a history after at most 10 10 steps and shares it across tested methods and seeds. PRE and POST then continue from the same snapshot D D , using the same agent, tools, environment, and eight-step limit; the repository’s FAIL_TO_PASS tests judge both outcomes. An instance-method pair is preserved when both continuations pass, damaged when PRE passes and POST fails, a rescue when PRE fails and POST passes, and unsolved when both fail. The paired labels preserve the direction of each change: damage identifies a lost full-history success, while rescue identifies a success reached from the summary after full-history failure. Reporting these separately prevents improvements on some repairs from cancelling losses on others in an aggregate success rate. First-round damage and rescue cases receive two additional seeds. A backbone case counts as stable damage when POST fails in at least two of its three runs; the prompt comparison uses one run per case. Appendix B reports the repeatability results. Recurring-Detail Retention measures literal preservation of structured values that occur both before an artificial boundary in a never-compacted session and in the next 3 3 to 8 8 request payloads. Future payloads include retransmitted history, so recurrence denotes continued presence in the interaction. Production-Chain Retention scores details found in the next at most 5 5 request payloads after each real compaction boundary, without requiring a match in the pre-boundary history. It also records whether a summary describes a completed file write as pending work. The two retention tracks use different boundaries for complementary purposes. Artificial boundaries allow the same recorded history to be summarized by multiple methods and scored against a common reference set. Production boundaries expose the summaries emitted during ongoing work, including successive replacements within one session. Task Preservation adds the execution outcome, so the benchmark reports both what remains in a summary and what the continuation accomplishes from it.

sections.heading: Task Preservation sample.
sections.text: The task set contains 35 localized SWE-bench repairs from 7 7 repositories: pytest ( 18 18 ), sympy ( 6 6 ), xarray ( 3 3 ), pylint ( 3 3 ), requests ( 2 2 ), sphinx ( 2 2 ), and flask ( 1 1 ). Selection favors fixes confined to one test file, few FAIL_TO_PASS tests, and a median gold patch below 1 1 KB. This concentrates evaluation on whether a continuation can turn the accumulated state into a specific repair. Each instance has a repository-specific environment recipe: Python 3.9 supports older repositories, while dependency constraints include numpy<2 for xarray, era-matched sphinxcontrib-* packages for sphinx, and py for pylint. Inclusion requires the base repository to fail the FAIL_TO_PASS tests and the gold patch to pass them. Appendix E provides instance-level tests and environment details.

sections.heading: Recurring-Detail Retention sample.
sections.text: This track uses 146 146 sessions from coding-agent harness trajectory: 73 73 Kimi Code, 50 50 Claude Code, 14 14 opencode, and 9 9 other clients, including 3 3 simulator-synthesized sessions. A candidate must have no detected compaction marker, at least 8 8 requests, a maximum recorded request-token count of at least 60,000 60{,}000 , and a completeness score of at least 0.8 0.8 . Completeness is the fraction of eligible adjacent request pairs that pass the history-prefix and cache-continuity checks in Appendix L . If a session has n n requests, where n n is the request count, the artificial boundary is placed at zero-based request index ⌊ 0.65 ​ n ⌋ \lfloor 0.65n\rfloor (rounding down); at least 3 3 requests must follow it, and at most 8 8 are included in the future window. Client quotas and ordering are in the supplementary configuration record. We exclude sessions with fewer than three matching details across the pre-boundary history and future payloads. The final set has 9,330 9{,}330 recurring details: paths, commit SHAs, pull-request identifiers, error types, URLs, key-value pairs, and IP addresses.

sections.heading: Production-Chain Retention sample.
sections.text: This track uses 106 106 sessions from the same corpus, each with at least two confirmed production compactions. They contain 224 224 boundaries: 106 106 first, 106 106 second, 10 10 third, and 2 2 fourth boundaries. At least one future detail can be evaluated at 140 140 boundaries ( 106 106 , 27 27 , 6 6 , and 1 1 at the respective boundary positions); only these enter detail-retention scores.

sections.heading: Reference prompts.
sections.text: The prompt comparison uses 5 5 production compaction prompts from coding-agent harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Kimi Code. They serve as reference methods in Task Preservation and Recurring-Detail Retention. Production-Chain Retention evaluates the summaries generated by the live systems in the recorded sessions.

sections.heading: Task Preservation.
sections.text: The damage rate is the fraction of PRE-pass cases that fail after compaction; the preservation rate is one minus this rate. Conditioning on full-history success identifies repairs that the continuation can complete before history replacement. The backbone comparison uses 22 22 validated PRE-pass cases among 24 24 evaluated cases; two are excluded because PRE failed in three re-run. We report preserved, damaged, rescued, and unsolved outcomes separately, using single-run results for the prompt comparison. For backbone cases selected for verification, stable damage requires POST failure in at least two of three runs.

sections.heading: Recurring-Detail Retention score.
sections.text: For any text T T (a history or request payload), let A ⁡ ( T ) A(T) be the deterministic extractor that returns distinct (type, value) pairs for paths, commit SHAs, pull-request or issue identifiers, error types, URLs, key-value pairs, and IP addresses. For session i i , let H i H_{i} be the pre-boundary history, F i F_{i} the concatenation of the next three to eight request payloads (including retransmitted history), and S i S_{i} the tested summary. The reference set A i = A ⁡ ( H i ) ∩ A ⁡ ( F i ) A_{i}=A(H_{i})\cap A(F_{i}) contains details extracted from both texts. A pair matches if its literal value occurs as a case-sensitive substring in S i S_{i} . The per-session score is retention i = matching pairs in ​ A i | A i | , \operatorname{retention}_{i}=\frac{\text{matching pairs in }A_{i}}{|A_{i}|}, where | ⋅ | |\cdot| denotes the number of elements in a set. Matching does not require a token boundary or the same type label in the summary. We report the unweighted mean of these session scores for each method; empty reference sets are excluded, and construction requires at least three reference details per session. Appendix L gives the extraction, normalization, and window rules.

sections.heading: Production-Chain Retention score.
sections.text: For session i i and its k k th compaction boundary, let F i , k F_{i,k} be the next at most five request payloads, S i , k S_{i,k} the production summary, and A i , k = A ⁡ ( F i , k ) A_{i,k}=A(F_{i,k}) the extracted future details. Here i i indexes sessions and k k is the boundary’s position within a session. Unlike the recurring-detail reference set, A i , k A_{i,k} does not require an intersection with pre-boundary history. As above, a detail pair matches when its value occurs as a case-sensitive substring in S i , k S_{i,k} . The score for a boundary is R i , k = matching detail pairs in ​ A i , k | A i , k | . R_{i,k}=\frac{\text{matching detail pairs in }A_{i,k}}{|A_{i,k}|}. We average these scores separately for first, second, and later boundaries, using only boundaries with at least one extracted future detail. We also report the mean last-to-first ratio within sessions where both boundaries have scores and the first-boundary score is nonzero: 22 sessions meet the two-boundary criterion and 20 remain after excluding zero first-boundary scores. For state-time disorder, the detector flags a boundary if a basename matched by the successful-write patterns in pre-boundary history as created or modified appears in the production summary within 150 characters of a pending-work phrase. We report this flag rate by boundary position over all boundaries, including those without extractable future details. Appendix L specifies the matching patterns and window.

sections.heading: 3.4 Evaluation Validation
sections.text: We check three properties before scoring: solvability (the gold patch passes in the supplied environment), discriminability (the base repository fails the FAIL_TO_PASS tests), and protocol validity (the agent and test judge use the same interpreter, and agent tests run against the live working tree).

sections.heading: Controlled replay.
sections.text: The agent and judge use the same per-instance interpreter, with PATH and PYTHONPATH pointing to the evaluation environment and live working tree. Phase A, PRE, and POST execute in the same directory, and the cached working-tree snapshot is restored before each continuation. This preserves the meaning of paths appearing in the history or summary and places both outcomes under the same conditions. Appendix D reports validation experiments for these controls.

sections.heading: Deterministic endpoints.
sections.text: Task outcomes use repository tests, and retention scores use deterministic extraction and string matching. Reference values are identified from recorded histories and future requests before comparing summaries. These endpoints provide instance-level evidence: a changed test verdict identifies task damage, while a missing literal value identifies detail loss. Auxiliary human validation of decision and progress labels is documented separately in Appendix D ; these labels do not enter the reported retention scores.

Damage rates use the 22 22 validated PRE-pass repairs. In the backbone study, first-round damage or rescue receives two additional runs ( K = 3 K{=}3 ); both PRE and POST are rerun for Kimi-K3, while other backbones reuse PRE. sections.heading: Agreement across repairs.
sections.text: The fourteen backbones agree on four of the 22 22 validated repairs and differ on the remaining 18 18 (Appendix A ). Every validated pytest repair and two of the three xarray repairs are damaged by at least one backbone, while the validated requests and pylint cases remain preserved throughout. Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserves 17 17 of the 18 18 repairs with disagreement. Its advantage is thus distributed across the disagreement set, with sphinx-9230 identifying a concrete case for which other summarizers supply a successful continuation state. The paired grid is useful precisely because these alternatives start from the same history and snapshot. A difficult repair need not fail under every summary: pytest-10081 has one preserving backbone, and sphinx-9230 has five. The benchmark thus localizes the configuration choices associated with success, while the aggregate rates quantify how frequently each choice preserves the tested repairs.

sections.heading: Effect of repeated runs.
sections.text: Repeated runs confirm 120 120 of the 126 126 first-round damaged instance–backbone pairs. GPT-6-Astra changes from 11 11 first-round damaged repairs to 9 9 confirmed cases; Claude Fable 5 5 , Qwen3.8-Max, GLM- 5.3 5.3 , and Hy4-Preview each change by one. Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 and DeepSeek-Flash remain the lowest- and highest-damage backbones. The broad spread between summarizers therefore persists under the confirmation rule, and most observed damage recurs across independent samples. Appendix B reports all observed outcomes for the selected cases.

sections.heading: What the retention gap measures.
sections.text: The mechanical anchor_index reference retains 79.1 % 79.1\% of recurring details, a 63.1 63.1 -percentage-point gap over the best LLM summary. These values are directly recoverable from recorded history under a bounded extraction procedure: the reference reads at most 400,000 400{,}000 serialized characters and keeps at most 40 40 values per type. The comparison quantifies how much recurring structured information survives extraction versus generated summarization. Task Preservation supplies the complementary execution test, assessing whether the resulting continuation state supports completing a repair. The retention reference gives each recurring value an explicit membership test, making omissions inspectable at the level of paths, identifiers, error types, or other extracted strings. Scores are averaged per session, so a session with many labels does not dominate the corpus mean. This consistently compares histories with different amounts of structured information. The joint results distinguish detail retention from task preservation. DeepSeek-Flash has the highest retention score under Claude Code but damages 14 14 of 22 22 repairs, compared with 4 4 for Kimi-K3. With Kimi-K3 fixed, Claude Code retains 15.0 % 15.0\% of recurring details versus 8.2 % 8.2\% for Kimi Code, while Kimi Code preserves one more repair. These are configuration-level comparisons across separate datasets. They show why evaluating both properties is useful: a configuration that preserves more recurring strings can still supply a less effective state for task continuation. The prompts also impose different output structures. Claude Code requests nine sections and produces summaries of about 10,000 10{,}000 characters on the retention set, compared with 1,600 − 5,200 1{,}600-5{,}200 for the other prompts. Kimi Code requests a first-person handoff focused on continuing the task. Thus, the observed prompt profiles combine differences in instructions, organization, and output length. Compact-Bench evaluates these production configurations as a whole, exposing how their information-retention and task-preservation outcomes differ.

sections.heading: Production-Chain Retention.
sections.text: Across 106 live sessions, mean retention is 15.7 % 15.7\% at the first boundary ( n = 106 n{=}106 ) and 19.9 % 19.9\% at the second ( n = 27 n{=}27 ); third- and fourth-boundary means are 4.9 % 4.9\% ( n = 6 n{=}6 ) and 1.8 % 1.8\% ( n = 1 n{=}1 ) (Figure 3 ). Each mean summarizes the evaluable subset at that position. The production measurements extend the benchmark from an artificial boundary to the summaries that agents actually receive during continued work. They document recurring-detail coverage across repeated history replacements, with per-session ratios and instruction-conditioned breakdowns in Appendix C . The first-boundary result covers all 106 106 sessions and places the controlled retention measurements alongside a deployed-use reference. Subsequent boundaries retain their own future-request windows, capturing the details present in the interaction after each replacement. This boundary-specific view preserves the context in which each production summary is used, rather than merging successive summaries into a single session-level artifact. sections.heading: From evidence to action.
sections.text: The sphinx-9230 trace makes that distinction visible in subsequent actions. PRE reads the target region, builds and checks a minimal reproduction, locates the call, and applies a short Python edit. POST reaches the relevant file, then searches broadly and reads test and reproduction code without making the repair. The trace contains 8 8 PRE tool actions and 13 13 POST actions within the shared eight-step budget, since a step can contain multiple tool actions (Appendix I ). Counts of explicit read_file calls show at most one repeat read per condition in each damaged case (Appendix J ). The observed divergence is in the transition from relevant evidence to an effective edit, even with the target file still accessible. This diagnosis illustrates the role of paired continuation in the benchmark. Retention scores locate missing details; paired traces reveal how a preserved or altered working state unfolds into subsequent actions. On the inspected repairs, the decisive outcome is executable task completion, and paths or code tokens provide evidence for interpreting that outcome. Combining these views makes it possible to distinguish a missing identifier from a continuation that still has the identifier but does not complete the repair.

sections.heading: Evaluation cost.
sections.text: The complete 35-repair study required about 8,000 model calls, with compression accounting for under 5 % 5\% of tokens. The main computational cost lies in generating and judging continuations, which provide the executable evidence for task preservation. Appendix G provides scoring rules, configurations, environment recipes, and instance-level outcome tables, supporting inspection of how each aggregate follows from its underlying cases.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Compact-Bench measures what survives context compaction through paired task continuation, recurring-detail matching, and real production chains. Its shared-boundary comparison separates summarizers by their ability to preserve executable repair progress: Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 has the lowest stable damage, with a 5 − 64 % 5-64\% range across fourteen backbones. Prompt choice also matters, with Kimi Code preserving the most repairs and Claude Code retaining the most recurring details under Kimi-K3. The paired failures establish the benchmark’s central distinction: retaining paths and code strings can coexist with losing the progress needed to finish a task. Evaluating both information and subsequent action makes that loss visible.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Results are conditional on the tested repository repairs, continuation agent, and budget. Detail-retention scores capture literal recurrence, while later production-boundary estimates use small, changing session subsets. Private session payloads and cached repair states are unavailable; Appendix G details the released scoring rules, configurations, and outcome tables.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: The Recurring-Detail Retention and Production-Chain Retention evaluations use real agentic sessions collected from online agent traffic on the authors’ institutional platform under its existing data-use agreements; sessions were analyzed in place and were not solicited from users for this study. The data was processed to extract structural items (paths, identifiers, error types) for labeling. The paper reports aggregate retention statistics; private session payloads and session-level label values are not distributed. Paths, URLs, and IP addresses can identify users or infrastructure; the distributed artifacts therefore exclude these private session-level values. Task Preservation reuses public SWE-bench instances under their original licenses. All reported experiments were run through metered API gateways under the authors’ institutional accounts. The benchmark is intended to help identify and reduce compaction-induced failures in deployed coding agents.

sections.heading: Availability and reproducibility.
sections.text: The accompanying compact-bench-reproducibility.zip supplies reference extraction and scoring code, transcript preprocessing, coding-agent inputs and tool schemas, environment recipes, and file schemas described in Appendix L . The Task Preservation first-round grids and selected additional runs (Appendices A , B , and F ) support recomputation of the reported task rates. The package excludes private session payloads, historical candidate order and sampling budget, and cached Task Preservation histories and working-tree snapshots. Recomputing session-level aggregates requires the source payloads; fresh Task Preservation runs generate new trajectories. The released rules and configurations specify the operations for implementing those evaluations.

sections.heading: Agent and tools.
sections.text: The continuation agent runs with two tools: read_file (confined to the working directory) and run_command with an allowlist ( pytest , python , grep , rg , cat , sed , head , tail , find , echo , cd , pwd , wc , diff , patch , git , mkdir , cp , mv , touch , pip , rm , ls ). Command outputs are truncated to 3,000 characters; file reads to 8,000. The agent’s shell receives the instance venv on PATH and the working directory on PYTHONPATH, so its python and pytest invocations exercise the live working tree with the judging interpreter.

sections.heading: Budgets and caching.
sections.text: Phase A allows at most 10 steps; each continuation at most 8; command timeout is 120s and test timeout is 300s. Compression inputs are preprocessed before the overall cap: in Task Preservation and cross-backbone runs, each text block is truncated to 2,000 characters and each tool input or output to 200 characters; in Recurring-Detail Retention, the limits are 4,000 and 500 characters; the serialized transcript is then capped at its last 250,000 characters. The anchor_index reference extracts from the first 400,000 characters of serialized history and keeps at most 40 values per type after sorting. Compression outputs are capped at 6,144 tokens for Kimi-K3 main runs and 16,384 tokens for cross-backbone and Recurring-Detail Retention runs. Each phase-A trajectory is cached and shared across methods and seeds; the working-directory snapshot is restored between PRE and POST.

sections.heading: Models and endpoints.
sections.text: Kimi-K3 and Claude-* models are called through the Anthropic messages endpoint; GPT-* models through the OpenAI chat-completions or responses endpoint, all via the same metered gateway with per-family API keys. Runs reported here were executed in September–October 2026 with gateway model identifiers kimi-k3 ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) , claude-opus-4-8 ( Anthropic, 2026c ) , claude-fable-5 ( Anthropic, 2026a ) , claude-fable-5-1 ( Anthropic, 2026b ) , gpt-5.6-luna ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , gpt-5.6-sol ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , gpt-5.6-terra ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , gpt-6-astra ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , claude-opus-5-5 ( Anthropic, 2026d ) , qwen3.8-max ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) , glm-5.3 ( Z.ai, 2026 ) , deepseek-v4-pro ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026b ; DeepSeek, 2026a ) , hy4-preview ( Tencent, 2026 ) , and deepseek-flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ; DeepSeek, 2026b ) . Kimi-K3 runs with thinking disabled; thinking-style models run with default settings. Continuation turns use max_tokens 4,096; compression output caps follow the preceding paragraph (6,144 for Kimi-K3 main runs, 16,384 for cross-backbone and Recurring-Detail Retention runs). The gateway offers no seed parameter, so seeds are independent server-side samples; temperature and other decoding settings are the service defaults, identical across conditions. Per-family environment pins follow fixed recipes: numpy<2 , pandas<2 , setuptools_scm<8 for xarray; py for pylint; docutils<0.18 and era-pinned sphinxcontrib-applehelp==1.0.2 , -devhelp==1.0.2 , -htmlhelp==2.0.0 , -qthelp==1.0.3 , -serializinghtml==1.1.5 for sphinx; plus pytest<8 , werkzeug<3 , and urllib3<2 everywhere. sections.heading: Appendix H Production Compaction Prompts
sections.text: The five production prompts are included verbatim below. The Claude Code prompt (634 characters) reads in full: Your task is to create a detailed summary of the conversation so far, paying close attention to the user’s explicit requests and your previous actions. This summary should be thorough in capturing technical details, code patterns, and architectural decisions that would be essential for continuing development work without losing context. Your summary should include the following sections: 1. Primary Request and Intent 2. Key Technical Concepts 3. Files and Code Sections (include full code snippets where applicable) 4. Errors and fixes 5. Problem Solving 6. All user messages 7. Pending Tasks 8. Current Work 9. Optional Next Step The opencode prompt (537 characters) reads in full: You are an anchored context summarization assistant for coding sessions. Summarize only the conversation history you are given. The newest turns may be kept verbatim outside your summary, so focus on the older context that still matters for continuing the work. Always follow the exact output structure requested by the user prompt. Keep every section, preserve exact file paths and identifiers when known, and prefer terse bullets over paragraphs. Do not answer the conversation itself. Respond in the same language as the conversation. The Codex prompt (423 characters) reads in full: You are performing a CONTEXT CHECKPOINT COMPACTION. Create a handoff summary for another LLM that will resume the task. Include: - Current progress and key decisions made - Important context, constraints, or user preferences - What remains to be done (clear next steps) - Any critical data, examples, or references needed to continue Be concise, structured, and focused on helping the next LLM seamlessly continue the work. The Kimi Code prompt (296 characters) reads in full: You are about to run out of context. Write a first-person handoff note to yourself so you can seamlessly continue this task after the earlier conversation is cleared. --- This message is a direct task, not part of the above conversation --- Write the note as your own continuing train of thought. The Gemini CLI prompt (279 characters) reads in full: You are an expert context compressor. Your job is to drastically shorten the following conversation while preserving the absolute core semantic meaning, facts, and intent. Omit all conversational filler, pleasantries, or redundant information. Return ONLY the compressed summary.

sections.heading: Contents and scope.
sections.text: The supplementary code implements transcript serialization, structured-value extraction, task labels, retention scoring, and completed-write detection as pure functions. Configuration files specify coding-agent inputs, tool schemas, budgets, and environment recipes; the instance manifest maps repairs to public commits and tests. Production prompts appear in Appendix H , and artifact availability is specified in Appendix G .

sections.heading: Session filtering.
sections.text: Within a session, the sessionizer sorts requests by timestamp and request identifier. Pairs crossing a new compaction marker or a token drop below half the preceding count are excluded from the completeness denominator. Other pairs must have matching nonempty first-200-character message prefixes. When token counts are available, the next cached-token count must be at least 80% of the preceding total; missing fields do not fail that check. Completeness is the passing fraction, or 1 with no eligible pairs, rounded to three decimals before filtering at 0.8.

sections.heading: Recurring-Detail Retention sampling and windows.
sections.text: Section 3.2 defines the eligibility filters and boundary index. For requested sample budget N N , the constructor takes the first ⌊ N / 3 ⌋ \lfloor N/3\rfloor candidates from Claude Code, ⌊ N / 2 ⌋ \lfloor N/2\rfloor from Kimi Code, and ⌊ N / 5 ⌋ \lfloor N/5\rfloor from each other client. Groups follow client-name order and the concatenation is capped at N N . Missing payloads and samples with fewer than three matching recurring details are then removed. Recurring-Detail Retention extracts structured values from the first 400,000 characters of Python JSON serialization with ensure_ascii=False . Future text concatenates the first 150,000 characters of each available message payload from at most eight requests, without history deduplication. Production-Chain Retention uses the same per-request cap over at most five requests and omits the history intersection.

sections.heading: Recurring-detail extraction and scoring.
sections.text: The module specifies path whitelists and exclusions, slash normalization, SHA and other identifier patterns, and URL truncation to 120 characters. Deduplication is within each kind; equal values in different kinds remain distinct labels. Hits use case-sensitive substring membership. Recurring-Detail Retention averages non-null per-session scores without weighting sessions by their number of labels. API/parse errors are excluded; returned empty summaries score zero. The mechanical reference keeps at most 40 sorted values per kind from the bounded history extraction.

sections.heading: Production-Chain Retention disorder and aggregation.
sections.text: Successful-write patterns scan the immediately preceding raw message payload. A detected file’s basename must occur within 150 characters on either side of a pending phrase in the summary; any match flags the boundary. Missing prior payloads and payloads with no detected writes are recorded as unflagged. The rate therefore measures contradictions captured by these patterns. All retained boundaries enter its denominator; boundaries with at least one evaluable detail enter retention. The last-to-first ratio divides the final retained boundary’s retention by the first non-null retention, excluding null final values and zero denominators. Every first boundary in the reported corpus is scorable. The module contains the literal multilingual patterns and summary-extraction rules.

Compact-Bench pairs full-history and summary-only continuations from a shared repository state, and evaluates recurring details and successive production compactions. It covers 35 35 SWE-bench repairs, 146 146 agentic sessions, and 106 106 production chains. Across 14 14 summarizer backbones, stable damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% of 22 22 full-history successes: Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserves the most repairs, while DeepSeek-Flash damages the most. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, the Kimi Code prompt preserves the most task continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). LLM summaries retain at most 16.0 % 16.0\% of recurring details, compared with 79.1 % 79.1\% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7 % 15.7\% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13 / 14 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation. Code and data are available online. 1 Introduction Long-horizon coding agents accumulate instructions, tool observations, test results, and partial decisions. Compaction allows them to work beyond the context window, but the resulting summary must carry enough state to resume unfinished work. Long-context benchmarks test retrieval, reasoning, and generation from extended inputs ( Bai et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Hsieh et al., 2024 ; Shaham et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Kuratov et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ) , and information access can depend on input position ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . Agent histories add a further requirement: preserving which actions have been taken, which hypotheses have been rejected, and what remains to be done. End-to-end benchmarks evaluate repository repair, code generation, and interactive tool use ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024c ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . A final score, however, does not isolate the effect of replacing a history midway through a task. Recent compaction evaluations examine constraint loss, archived-fact retrieval, future-trajectory support, and execution instability; methods also learn or schedule summarization and remove observations ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Subramani, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Cim et al., 2026 ; Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . Compact-Bench targets the history replacement itself: it compares full-history and summary-only continuation at a shared boundary, then examines detail retention in real agent sessions. The benchmark asks: For the same task and pre-compaction state, how does continuation change when an agent receives only a summary instead of its full history? Task Preservation compares full-history and summary-only continuations from the same repository snapshot, using the same agent, step budget, and executable tests. Recurring-Detail Retention measures preservation of structured details that recur in later requests across 146 146 sessions ( 143 143 real and 3 3 simulator-synthesized). Production-Chain Retention follows these details across successive compactions in 106 106 real sessions. Together, the three evaluations connect controlled task outcomes with information retention in deployed workflows. Across 14 14 summarizer backbones, stable Task Preservation damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% of the 22 22 validated full-history successes, with Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserving the most repairs. Of 126 126 instance-backbone pairs damaged in the first round, 120 120 meet the three-run confirmation criterion. Task preservation and detail retention also distinguish different configurations: Kimi Code gives the most passing continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). Paired traces reveal a shared failure pattern: summaries can retain the target file and relevant strings while losing the progress needed to finish a repair. Overall, our contributions are: • We introduce Compact-Bench , a benchmark for evaluating whether context compaction preserves a coding agent’s ability to resume work. It combines controlled task continuations with recurring-detail and production-chain measurements. • We compare 14 14 summarizer backbones and 5 5 production prompts. Stable task damage ranges from 5 − 64 % 5-64\% among 22 22 full-history successes, with Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 preserving the most repairs. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, Kimi Code preserves the most task continuations ( 19 / 22 19/22 ), while Claude Code retains the most recurring details ( 15.0 % 15.0\% ). • We show that retained repair evidence does not guarantee successful continuation. Paired traces reveal failures even when summaries preserve target files and relevant code strings. Together with the different task-preservation and detail-retention leaders, this finding motivates evaluating compaction through both retained information and agent behavior. ReSum summarizes search trajectories; Context-Folding condenses completed subtasks; CompactionRL trains execution and summarization jointly; SelfCompact lets the agent choose when to compact; and parallel compaction summarizes separate blocks ( Wu et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026a ; Cim et al., 2026 ) . Compact-Bench extends the evaluation target to resuming agent work, combining executable outcomes with deterministic matching of recurring details. 3 Compact-Bench 3.1 Evaluation Dimensions Let H H denote the serialized agent history immediately before a compaction boundary. The compaction method under test, denoted by C C , includes the summarizer and prompt together with the fixed serialization and truncation procedure described in Appendix G ; applying it to H H produces summary S = C ⁡ ( H ) S=C(H) . A compaction boundary is the point at which this replacement occurs. In Task Preservation, PRE continues with the full history H H , whereas POST continues with only S S . Both conditions start from the same repository working-tree snapshot, denoted by D D in Figure 1 . Task Preservation tests whether continuation from S S completes repairs that also succeed from H H . For each repair, Phase A caches a history after at most 10 10 steps and shares it across tested methods and seeds. PRE and POST then continue from the same snapshot D D , using the same agent, tools, environment, and eight-step limit; the repository’s FAIL_TO_PASS tests judge both outcomes. An instance-method pair is preserved when both continuations pass, damaged when PRE passes and POST fails, a rescue when PRE fails and POST passes, and unsolved when both fail. The paired labels preserve the direction of each change: damage identifies a lost full-history success, while rescue identifies a success reached from the summary after full-history failure. Reporting these separately prevents improvements on some repairs from cancelling losses on others in an aggregate success rate. First-round damage and rescue cases receive two additional seeds. A backbone case counts as stable damage when POST fails in at least two of its three runs; the prompt comparison uses one run per case. Appendix B reports the repeatability results. Recurring-Detail Retention measures literal preservation of structured values that occur both before an artificial boundary in a never-compacted session and in the next 3 3 to 8 8 request payloads. Future payloads include retransmitted history, so recurrence denotes continued presence in the interaction. Production-Chain Retention scores details found in the next at most 5 5 request payloads after each real compaction boundary, without requiring a match in the pre-boundary history. It also records whether a summary describes a completed file write as pending work. The two retention tracks use different boundaries for complementary purposes. Artificial boundaries allow the same recorded history to be summarized by multiple methods and scored against a common reference set. Production boundaries expose the summaries emitted during ongoing work, including successive replacements within one session. Task Preservation adds the execution outcome, so the benchmark reports both what remains in a summary and what the continuation accomplishes from it. 3.2 Data and Construction Evaluation Size Composition Task Preservation 35 instances Localized SWE-bench repairs from 7 repositories: pytest (18), sympy (6), xarray (3), pylint (3), requests (2), sphinx (2), and flask (1). Phase A, PRE, and POST execute in the same directory, and the cached working-tree snapshot is restored before each continuation. This preserves the meaning of paths appearing in the history or summary and places both outcomes under the same conditions. Appendix D reports validation experiments for these controls. Deterministic endpoints. Task outcomes use repository tests, and retention scores use deterministic extraction and string matching. Reference values are identified from recorded histories and future requests before comparing summaries. These endpoints provide instance-level evidence: a changed test verdict identifies task damage, while a missing literal value identifies detail loss. This diagnosis illustrates the role of paired continuation in the benchmark. Retention scores locate missing details; paired traces reveal how a preserved or altered working state unfolds into subsequent actions. On the inspected repairs, the decisive outcome is executable task completion, and paths or code tokens provide evidence for interpreting that outcome. Appendix G provides scoring rules, configurations, environment recipes, and instance-level outcome tables, supporting inspection of how each aggregate follows from its underlying cases. 5 Conclusion Compact-Bench measures what survives context compaction through paired task continuation, recurring-detail matching, and real production chains. Its shared-boundary comparison separates summarizers by their ability to preserve executable repair progress: Claude Opus 4.8 4.8 has the lowest stable damage, with a 5 − 64 % 5-64\% range across fourteen backbones. Prompt choice also matters, with Kimi Code preserving the most repairs and Claude Code retaining the most recurring details under Kimi-K3. The paired failures establish the benchmark’s central distinction: retaining paths and code strings can coexist with losing the progress needed to finish a task. Evaluating both information and subsequent action makes that loss visible. Limitations Results are conditional on the tested repository repairs, continuation agent, and budget. Detail-retention scores capture literal recurrence, while later production-boundary estimates use small, changing session subsets. Private session payloads and cached repair states are unavailable; Appendix G details the released scoring rules, configurations, and outcome tables. The data was processed to extract structural items (paths, identifiers, error types) for labeling. The paper reports aggregate retention statistics; private session payloads and session-level label values are not distributed. Paths, URLs, and IP addresses can identify users or infrastructure; the distributed artifacts therefore exclude these private session-level values. The continuation agent runs with two tools: read_file (confined to the working directory) and run_command with an allowlist ( pytest , python , grep , rg , cat , sed , head , tail , find , echo , cd , pwd , wc , diff , patch , git , mkdir , cp , mv , touch , pip , rm , ls ). Command outputs are truncated to 3,000 characters; file reads to 8,000. The agent’s shell receives the instance venv on PATH and the working directory on PYTHONPATH, so its python and pytest invocations exercise the live working tree with the judging interpreter.
